question: Raw water cools to 2 degrees C in January. What change in the water itself makes floc settling slower than it was in the fall?
correctAnswer: The water becomes more viscous, so floc particles settle more slowly
explanation: Cold water is more viscous, and that resistance slows particle settling, so basins perform differently in winter even at the same coagulant dose.
options: The water becomes more viscous, so floc particles settle more slowly
The water becomes less viscous, so floc particles settle much more quickly
The water loses its alkalinity completely, so no floc can form at all in the basin
The water becomes dense with dissolved gas, so floc floats instead of settling down
sourceTitle: US EPA - Small Drinking Water Systems Handbook
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Coagulation Under Cold Water Conditions. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: The water becomes more viscous, so floc particles settle more slowly
optionB: The water becomes less viscous, so floc particles settle much more quickly
optionC: The water loses its alkalinity completely, so no floc can form at all in the basin
optionD: The water becomes dense with dissolved gas, so floc floats instead of settling down

question: A gravity filter is returned to service after backwashing. Why does effluent turbidity start high and then improve over the first part of the run?
correctAnswer: Clean media has not yet collected retained solids that help capture new particles
explanation: During ripening the freshly washed grains capture particles poorly at first; as solids collect on the media, capture improves and effluent turbidity falls.
options: Backwash water left in the clearwell is being pushed backward through the clean media bed
The media grains have swollen shut, forcing all the flow through a few open channels in the bed
Air from the backwash keeps lifting settled solids off the media surface for the rest of the run
Clean media has not yet collected retained solids that help capture new particles
sourceTitle: US EPA: Surface Water Treatment Rules — supporting treatment resources
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Filter Ripening and Turbidity Spikes. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: Backwash water left in the clearwell is being pushed backward through the clean media bed
optionB: The media grains have swollen shut, forcing all the flow through a few open channels in the bed
optionC: Air from the backwash keeps lifting settled solids off the media surface for the rest of the run
optionD: Clean media has not yet collected retained solids that help capture new particles

question: A storage tank fills and drains through pipes at the same end of the tank. What operating problem can that arrangement create inside the tank?
correctAnswer: Water short circuits, so older water can sit for long periods in dead zones
explanation: Inlet and outlet at one end let fresh water leave quickly while distant water ages, loses residual, and can develop quality problems.
options: Water mixes too completely, so chlorine residual builds up instead of decaying over time
Water short circuits, so older water can sit for long periods in dead zones
Water near the far wall freezes solid in summer because it moves faster than the rest
Water pressure inside the tank doubles because both pipes push against the same wall
sourceTitle: US EPA - Small Drinking Water Systems Handbook
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Storage and Distribution Interface. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: Water mixes too completely, so chlorine residual builds up instead of decaying over time
optionB: Water short circuits, so older water can sit for long periods in dead zones
optionC: Water near the far wall freezes solid in summer because it moves faster than the rest
optionD: Water pressure inside the tank doubles because both pipes push against the same wall
